headline: Nvidia beats after a bruising day, but the bounce has to survive Europe's open
tone: Risk-off into the close: the US open's chip bounce faded, Europe had its worst day since March, and the Dow led the losses. Nvidia's beat after the bell takes the worst-case off the table, but it doesn't answer the leadership and China questions that drove the sell-off.
body: The US open's bounce didn't hold. Selling picked up in the afternoon, and stocks hit their lows after CNN reported that a classified NSA network had gone down. Sources said there was no sign of a cyberattack, but it came on top of last week's Outlook outage and the weekend FAA ground stop, so traders sold first. The S&P 500 closed at its lowest since late July and the Nasdaq briefly touched its lowest since April. Nvidia itself flipped between gains and losses and closed slightly lower, despite a brief lift when Jensen Huang said he would be open to returning as CEO.

Nvidia then cleared the bar with room to spare. Revenue was $115.8bn against about $109bn expected, data centre revenue was $107.6bn, and fourth-quarter guidance of $130bn (plus or minus 3%) beat the roughly $125bn consensus, even though it assumes no China data-centre revenue. The stock rose 2-3% after hours. Options had priced a 7-8% swing either way, so the reaction is modest. Margins are guided down to 71-72% from 74.9%, and interim CEO Colette Kress still has to deal with the Huang and export-control questions on the call.

Europe closed before the beat and took the full hit. Tech had its worst day since February, led by ASML, after Washington widened its AI-chip licence rules to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. Deutsche Bank fell 6% on leaked client documents, and miners slid as weak Chinese data weighed on copper. Oil and gas was the most resilient sector, because crude reversed early losses on the Qeshm Island strikes and more mine hits near Hormuz. Gulf flows are back near pre-war levels, though, which caps how far each headline can lift crude.

Rates: Williams said more hikes are likely and warned that AI investment could keep inflation sticky into 2027, but he ruled out 'dramatic action', which pushes back on Waller's case for a 50bp move. A 25bp hike on 9 December is still the base case. Priced in for tomorrow: a relief open in chips and in Europe's tech names. What would change that: a cautious Kress on the call, or more infrastructure-outage headlines. Then EIA crude stocks on Wednesday and Anthropic's listing on Thursday become the next tests for the AI trade.

views.text: Nvidia's beat should lift Europe's chip names at the open, because ASML and the equipment makers never got to trade it. But a beat already partly priced by options, plus a lower margin guide, argues for a relief bounce rather than a trend change until the leadership and China questions are settled.

Fed speakers stayed hawkish but measured: Williams backs further gradual hikes, Hammack spoke on Treasury-market backstops rather than rates, and Waller avoided monetary policy. Nothing today moved the December 25bp base case, so the dollar is taking its cue from risk appetite rather than the Fed.
